column4: This explicitly names the warned people's “evil morning” when punishment descends on their courtyard, giving the image's dawn raid its Qur'anic counterpart as a sudden punitive arrival at home.
Lot is told to leave by night because the people's appointed time is morning; this makes the night journey and near dawn arrival a concrete parallel to the section's raid timetable.
The cry catches the people of al-Hijr as they enter morning; its sudden morning seizure directly echoes the section's dawn strike and raised cry.
The text says punishment “came upon them early in the morning” (بُكْرَةً), using ṣ-b-ḥ, the source section's named morning root, for a settled doom that overtakes people at daybreak.
A cry seizes the wrongdoers and leaves them fallen in their homes by morning; the home-bound victims and morning vocal shock closely parallel the section's vulnerable encampment and alarm cry.
The people of Midian are taken by the cry and found fallen in their homes by morning, another specific pairing of sudden vocal punishment with its dawn aftermath.
The people are caught by a shout at sunrise; 15:74 completes this same Lot episode with the city overturned and stones, while this row contributes the morning shout.
This asks whether town people feel secure from divine force arriving at night while they sleep; it directly recalls the section's account of attackers timing their approach for an unready camp.
Destroyed towns are struck at night or while their people sleep at midday; the verse supplies the broader Qur'anic image of punishment reaching a settlement during vulnerable hours.
God may seize wrongdoers during their ordinary activity, and they cannot escape; this matches the section's claim that a charge into the gathered crowd leaves no room to flee.

Satan is told to come against people with “your cavalry and infantry” (بِخَيْلِكَ وَرَجِلِكَ); this is the Qur'an's direct mounted-and-footed assault image corresponding to the section's riders charging a people.

Ready horses are kept to deter God's enemy and the community's enemy (عَدُوَّكُمْ); this uses mounted force in the same military scene but as prepared deterrence, a boundary against the surprise assault described here.
Lot's people rush toward him to seize his guests; their bodily rush on a target concretely parallels the source gloss for th-w-r, “people leapt upon him,” and the assault into a crowd.
The mob states its intent toward Lot's guests, making explicit the predatory purpose behind the rushing crowd in 11:78; this sharpens the section's attack-on-a-community image.
The people of the city arrive at Lot's house rejoicing over his guests; this begins a second account of a crowd converging on a vulnerable household.
Lot's visitors ask whether he was not forbidden from receiving people; this exposes the hostile crowd's effort to control and menace those under his protection.
The preceding question asks whether the rejecters are hastening the punishment; 37:177 supplies the bad morning that answers it, linking demanded punishment to its abrupt arrival.
The verse fixes shares of what was taken as booty (غَنِمْتُمْ); it directly contextualizes the source's lexical note that a naqīʿa is meat taken from plunder before division.

It permits eating from what was captured as booty (غَنِمْتُمْ); this is a specific food-and-spoils parallel to the source's pre-division slaughter term, though the verse does not itself prescribe that custom.
The question about spoils and the command to set relations right place the raid's aftermath in a Qur'anic dispute over booty and its allocation.
After the readiness against enemies in 8:60, this commands accepting an enemy's move toward peace; it supplies an adjacent limit on continuing a mounted attack.
The command “do not transgress” (تَعْتَدُوا) uses the aggression root named in the section's gloss of ʿudwān as manifest injustice, and sets a clear limit on fighting even in a military encounter.
It locates blame on those who wrong people and transgress in the land without right, closely matching the section's explicit gloss of ʿudwān as plain injustice.
The verse forbids hostility over being barred from the Sacred Mosque from turning into transgression; it gives a concrete moral boundary for the section's assault-and-injustice reading.

Even hatred of a people must not lead believers away from justice; this checks the slide from identifying someone as an enemy to treating them unjustly, a distinction raised by the section's ʿaduww/ʿudwān note.
Permission to fight is given to people who are themselves fought because they were wronged; this sharply distinguishes a just defense from the section's morally charged image of aggression.

The verse says that a person once marked by enmity can become “as a devoted friend” (وَلِيٌّ حَمِيمٌ) when evil is repelled with good; it directly complicates the section's lexical pairing of enemy and friend.
The verse pairs “My enemy and your enemy” with taking them as allies (أَوْلِيَاءَ), directly staging the enemy/friend opposition noted in the source, in a concrete plot against the Messenger.
It says God may place affection between believers and those they currently oppose; this is a specific reversal of the enemy relation named in the section.

The verse describes meeting an enemy in battle, striking, then binding captives; it concretely fits the source's secondary sh-d-d sense of charging an enemy, while its context is open battle rather than a dawn raid.
This continues the morning appointment in 11:81 with the command arriving and the town overturned; it contributes the execution of the threatened blow, not the timing itself.
After the sunrise shout in 15:73, the city is turned upside down and stones fall; this completes the sudden strike in the cited row's account.

The companion warning asks whether town people feel safe from divine force at midday while playing; it extends the sleeping-at-night warning of 7:97 into a different unguarded hour than the section's dawn.
It asks who besides wrongdoers would be destroyed if God's punishment came suddenly or openly; the two modes clarify the section's sudden dawn assault as one form of an openly destructive arrival.
The warning says punishment may arrive suddenly while people do not perceive it; this articulates the section's specific surprise-and-unpreparedness theme in judgment language.
During the Confederates' siege, the enemy comes from above and below and the believers' eyes and hearts react in terror; it reverses the cavalry's role, showing the panic of a beset community.
The siege in 33:10 becomes a severe shaking of the believers; this row contributes the inner effect of being pressed by the gathered enemy forces.

Lot wishes he had strength or a firm support against the rushing crowd; رُكْنٍ شَدِيدٍ uses the source's sh-d-d root for support/strength, not its secondary “charge at an enemy” sense, making a precise reversal of attacker and unprotected target.
Lot calls the crowd's attention to his guests and asks them not to disgrace him; the household under attack is the vulnerable side of the same crowd-convergence scene.
Lot invokes fear of God as the alternative to shaming and assaulting his guests, putting a moral restraint beside the section's root gloss of aggression as injustice.
The verse recalls that people were enemies before God joined their hearts; it gives a concrete reversal of the ʿaduww relation that the section defines against friendship.

This lists adorned horses among coveted worldly goods; it connects the section's cavalry and its surrounding reference to love of wealth with a Qur'anic pairing of horses and material desire, although these horses are prized possessions rather than attackers.

The source links 100:8's شديد to an enemy-charge sense, while this verse uses the same sh-d-d root for those whose love of God is stronger; the distinct sense and object of intensity are a specific, if indirect, counterpoint.

A calamity reaches the garden owners while they sleep, and 68:21–25 show them setting out early to find the loss; this is a dawn-vulnerability parallel, though it concerns a ruined orchard rather than an attacking force.

The garden owners call to one another at daybreak after the nocturnal calamity of 68:19; the awakening-at-dawn timing parallels the raid's vulnerable hour, while the event is a crop's destruction rather than combat.

They set out early, confident and determined, only to find their garden ruined in 68:26; this reverses the section's confident mounted advance, but the connection is the dawn-discovered loss rather than a shared raid scene.

The preceding question asks whether plotters feel secure from punishment arriving where they do not perceive it; 16:46 adds seizure during activity and no escape, so this row contributes the unexpectedness behind the section's blow.
In the same Lot episode as 54:38, a stone storm is sent against the people while Lot's family is saved before dawn; it adds the concrete attack and dawn rescue behind the cited morning punishment.
The people press Lot for access to his guests and are blinded; this is a specific mob assault on protected visitors, echoing the source's secondary th-w-r sense of people leaping upon a target.

On the Day of Resurrection a person asks where escape is; this directly matches the section's claim that the charge into the crowd marks the moment with nowhere left to flee, and its explicit turn toward the final day.
The answer to the escape question in 75:10 is that there is no refuge; this verse supplies the inescapability that the section makes central to its dawn-strike image.

Continuing the fighting rules near 2:190, it says that if opponents cease there is to be no aggression (عُدْوَانَ) except against wrongdoers; this gives the section's ʿudwān root a precise boundary in a combat context.
God permits kindness and justice toward people who have not fought the believers or driven them from home; this limits the section's enemy/friend distinction by the actual conduct of the other party.
The next verse forbids taking as allies those who fought, expelled, or aided expulsion; it identifies the concrete hostile conduct that distinguishes an enemy from those addressed in 60:8.
This completes the Lot destruction begun in 11:82 by identifying its marked stones and saying the punishment is not far from wrongdoers; it adds the judgment's specific target and warning.
This follows the morning cry in 15:83 by saying that the people of al-Hijr's earnings did not avail them; it states that resources could not protect the struck community.

At Uhud, the fighting group falters and divides between desire for this world and the Hereafter; this is a battle-context counterpoint to the section's link from a cavalry charge and spoils to intense attachment to worldly “good.”

The people of the fortified houses think their strongholds will protect them, yet removal comes unexpectedly and terror is cast into their hearts; this is a specific reversal of the section's unprepared encampment, with confidence in defenses replacing sleep.

Garden owners swear to go early and harvest, but the overnight calamity in the surrounding passage ruins their plan; this is a specific dawn-going reversal of the section's successful dawn assault, though it is a harvest rather than combat.

They explicitly plan to keep a poor person out of the garden; this is a specific but indirect boundary on the source's booty-sharing detail, since the verse concerns hoarded produce rather than war spoils.

One member described as the group's “middle” or most judicious person rebukes the others after their loss; the root w-s-ṭ shifts from the source's physical center of a crowd to a moral voice within a group.

The source's w-s-ṭ describes cavalry entering the physical center of a gathered crowd; this verse uses the same root for a community characterized as balanced and just, an indirect contrast between occupying a group's center and serving as its ethical middle.
